newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: PowerSeraya becomes Singapore's top power producer.
newsitem.headline: PowerSeraya becomes Singapore's top power producer.

text.p: PowerSeraya Ltd, a unit of state gas and utility Singapore Power (SP), has become the country's largest power company with the completion of a new plant, SP chairman Ho Kwon Ping said on Tuesday.
He told reporters PowerSeraya now planned to redevelop the 810-megawatt (MW) Jurong power station as part of its plans to be competitive when Singapore deregulates the power industry next year.
"With a combined generating capacity of 2,980 megawatts Power Seraya is now the biggest power generation company in Singapore, catering to 50 percent of Singapore power's needs," Ho said.
He was speaking at the official opening of the S$1.1 billion (US$764 million) 250 MW generator plant on Pulau Seraya, off the southwest coast of Singapore.
He said PowerSeraya would have to improve its efficiency in order to stay competitive and maintain its market share.

"It is going to be a free market," Ho said. "I think it is the job of the regulator to ensure that there is a competitive situation and not a complete oversupply. We, however, being the the largest producer, are prepared to be very competitive under any circumstance."
PowerSeraya managing director Shum Siew Keong said he did not foresee overcapacity in power generation in Singapore.
"Singapore can take it," Shum said. "The current growth rate is roughly six to seven percent so the expansion of capacity has to be six to seven percent."
"By the year 2000, we are talking of a range of 5,000 MW demand for Singapore," he added "The installed capacity has to be more for the spinning reserve."

PowerSeraya, which operates power stations on Pulau Seraya and at Jurong on the southwest coast of Singapore, plans to replace units at the 30-year old Jurong Power Station with a combined cycle plant by 2001 or 2002 of a similar capacity.

"Our licensed capacity is fixed by the regulator so when we revamp, we have to replace the capacity of 810 MW," Shum said. "We have to apply to the regulator for them to allow us to expand the capacity and that we cannot forsee at the moment."
He estimated the cost of conversion at around $800 million.
Shum also said SP was talking to Indonesia's state-owned Petronas and Malaysia's Pertamina on possible gas supplies for the revamped plant.
